## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

{{< include ../learning_objectives/0532-virtual-environments-python-uv-run.qmd >}}

## Two ways to use an environment

The uv chapters run everything through `uv run`:

- scripts, `uv run penguins.py`
- JupyterLab, `uv run jupyter lab`
- Quarto, `uv run quarto render`
- tests, `uv run pytest`

Many tutorials, and some tools, *activate* the environment instead.

This chapter shows what each one does,
using the `penguin_analysis` project from [uv: projects](0530-virtual-environments-python-uv-projects.qmd),
and gives you a good way to think about `uv run`.

## Activating, running, deactivating

In a new terminal, `python3` is whatever Python your computer finds first.
On this Mac that is Homebrew's:

```bash
which python3
```

```out
/opt/homebrew/bin/python3
```

Activating the project's environment changes that:

::: {.panel-tabset group="shell"}
## macOS and Linux

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
```

## Windows (Git Bash)

```bash
source .venv/Scripts/activate
```

## Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
```
:::

Your prompt now starts with `(penguin-analysis)`,
and every command you type finds the environment first:

```bash
which python3
echo $VIRTUAL_ENV
```

```out
/Users/dan/penguin_analysis/.venv/bin/python3
/Users/dan/penguin_analysis/.venv
```

Activating did two things.
It put `.venv/bin` first on your `PATH`
(`.venv\Scripts` on Windows),
and it set the `VIRTUAL_ENV` environment variable to the environment's folder.
Python's own documentation describes these two changes in
[How venvs work](https://docs.python.org/3/library/venv.html#how-venvs-work).
Now `python penguins.py`, `jupyter lab` and `quarto render` all use the project's packages:

```bash
python penguins.py
```

```out
  species     island  bill_length_mm  ...  body_mass_g     sex  year
0  Adelie  Torgersen            39.1  ...       3750.0    male  2007
1  Adelie  Torgersen            39.5  ...       3800.0  female  2007
...
```

The environment stays active until you deactivate it
or close the terminal:

```bash
deactivate
which python3
```

```out
/opt/homebrew/bin/python3
```

## A good way to think about `uv run`

uv's documentation says that `uv run` runs a command in the project environment,
and that before every `uv run`,
uv checks that `uv.lock` matches `pyproject.toml`
and that `.venv` matches `uv.lock`
([Running commands](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/guides/projects/#running-commands)).
The same guide gives the alternative to `uv run`.
You run `uv sync`, then activate the environment, then run your command.

So a good way to think about `uv run <command>` is as a shortcut for four steps:

1. `uv sync`, so `.venv` matches `uv.lock`
2. activate the environment
3. run the command
4. deactivate the environment

uv's documentation does not describe how `uv run` sets up the environment internally.
You can see, though, that for the command it runs,
it changes the same two things activating does:

```bash
uv run python -c "import os, sys; print(sys.executable); print(os.environ['VIRTUAL_ENV'])"
which python3
```

```out
/Users/dan/penguin_analysis/.venv/bin/python
/Users/dan/penguin_analysis/.venv
/opt/homebrew/bin/python3
```

Inside `uv run`, Python is the project's,
and `VIRTUAL_ENV` names the project's `.venv`.
Straight afterwards, `python3` is Homebrew's again.
There is nothing to deactivate,
because nothing stayed active.

So these do the same work:

::: {.panel-tabset group="shell"}
## macOS and Linux

```bash
uv sync
source .venv/bin/activate
python penguins.py
deactivate
```

## Windows (Git Bash)

```bash
uv sync
source .venv/Scripts/activate
python penguins.py
deactivate
```

## Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
uv sync
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
python penguins.py
deactivate
```
:::

```bash
uv run penguins.py
```

## What `uv run` does that activating does not

Before it runs your command,
`uv run` makes sure `.venv` matches `uv.lock`,
and creates `.venv` if it does not exist yet
(uv's [`uv run` reference](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/reference/cli/#uv-run) says
"the project environment will be created and updated before invoking the command").
Activating only switches to whatever `.venv` already holds.

The difference shows in a fresh clone of the project,
which has `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` and the code,
but no `.venv`:

```bash
source .venv/bin/activate
```

```out
bash: .venv/bin/activate: No such file or directory
```

```bash
uv run penguins.py
```

```out
Using CPython 3.14.3
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Installed 5 packages in 72ms
  species     island  bill_length_mm  ...  body_mass_g     sex  year
0  Adelie  Torgersen            39.1  ...       3750.0    male  2007
1  Adelie  Torgersen            39.5  ...       3800.0  female  2007
2  Adelie  Torgersen            40.3  ...       3250.0  female  2007
3  Adelie  Torgersen             NaN  ...          NaN     NaN  2007
4  Adelie  Torgersen            36.7  ...       3450.0  female  2007

[5 rows x 8 columns]
```

| | Activate, run, deactivate | `uv run` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finds the environment's Python and programs | yes | yes |
| How long it lasts | until `deactivate` or the terminal closes | one command |
| Checks `.venv` against `uv.lock` first | no | yes |
| Creates `.venv` if it is missing | no | yes |

## Which to use

Use `uv run` for scripts, JupyterLab, Quarto and tests,
and put those commands in your Makefile targets.
You never have to remember which environment is active,
and the environment always matches the lockfile.

Activating is fine when a tool expects an active environment,
or when you want to type many commands in a row.
Run `uv sync` first, so `.venv` matches `uv.lock`,
and `deactivate` when you are done.
A forgotten `deactivate` leaves the environment active
for whatever you run next in that terminal,
even in another project.
[uv: rendering Quarto documents](0550-virtual-environments-python-uv-quarto.qmd)
shows that happening with a Quarto report.
